title: V-Mem: Modality-Routed Retrieval for Long-Term Multimodal Agentic Memory

visual_explainer.blocker: Fresh isolated V-Mem visual backfill on 2026-08-12 failed Visual QA after three GPT Image renders. Each render materially deviated from the full paper: it changed the paper title/subtitle, modeled an impossible image-only query instead of V-Mem's four query/target modality cases, mislabeled the Mem-Gallery LLM-judge ablation as accuracy, genericized the actual SigLIP/anchor mechanisms, and introduced unsupported framing. Because these errors could misstate both mechanism and evidence, no WebP was published. GitHub binary transport is available; the blocker is GPT Image grounding/faithfulness for this figure.

analysis.tldr: V-Mem treats multimodal memory retrieval as a routing problem: search within a modality, cross modalities through shared conversational rounds, and synthesize a search anchor when the raw query is not similar to the evidence that answers it.
analysis.problem: Multimodal histories break the usual similarity-search assumption twice: text and image evidence are separated by a modality gap, and the most query-similar item can still differ from the evidence needed to answer the question.
analysis.core_idea: Keep raw conversations as rounds with separate text and image lanes, infer query and target-evidence modality, retrieve within the appropriate lane, use same-round binding for cross-modal lookup, and generate hypothetical captions or image-enriched text anchors when raw similarity is insufficient.

memory_design.write: Append raw conversational rounds without LLM summarization or fact extraction; build text dense/BM25 indexes and an image embedding lane while preserving raw images and round bindings.
memory_design.organize: Represent memory as chronological rounds containing modality-specific units, with text and image retrieval lanes connected by shared-round identity rather than one joint vector space.
memory_design.read: Route by query modality and inferred target modality, perform lane-specific retrieval and rank fusion, cross modalities by returning content from matched rounds, optionally generate a query-side anchor, and include neighboring rounds when useful.
memory_design.update_forget: Memory construction is incremental append; the paper does not introduce consolidation, conflict repair, or forgetting beyond retrieval-time selection.

compared_to: Omni-SimpleMem as a multimodalized extraction/retrieval baseline
A-Mem-style structured memory under matched backbones and encoders
analysis.evidence: On Mem-Gallery with gpt-4o-mini, V-Mem reports 0.825 LLM-judge score versus 0.561 for the strongest baseline, and 0.872 on provided-image questions where no baseline exceeds 0.472. On LoCoMo it reports 0.690 versus 0.583. The incremental ablation is especially informative: vanilla retrieval scores 0.680, routing 0.689, shared-round matching 0.818, and generated anchors 0.825, making shared-round structure the load-bearing component. Build-time memory construction uses zero LLM tokens, although answer-time context can be larger than some baselines.
analysis.why_it_matters: It fills a real access-interface gap in current agent memory: richer modalities do not necessarily need a more universal embedding space; preserving interaction structure and routing to modality-specific operators can be more important than cross-modal similarity itself.
limitations: Target-modality routing partly relies on query-form heuristics, so ambiguous information needs may be misrouted.
The generated-anchor component gives only a small aggregate gain after shared-round matching and can hurt some text-to-text cases.
Evaluation is still long-term conversation QA rather than an acting multimodal agent whose memory affects tools or environment behavior.
Open-domain LoCoMo questions are weaker than M2A in the reported breakdown, and results vary with smaller vision-language backbones.
